**Opening Argument for Debater B: C = 992/2069**

The adversary's best strategy is to make every person identical. When weight vectors match, the selector can only choose how many people go to each color. Differences between people would give the selector extra freedom, such as swapping assignments, which can only lower the maximum load.

With g colors at weight a and 66−g colors at weight b, the selector splits the 2025 people into groups of size about 32 and 31. Balancing the loads gives 32a = 31b. The feasibility condition, which requires m to satisfy both ceiling constraints, holds exactly when g ≤ 2025 − 30·66 − 2 = 43. So g = 43 is the largest feasible choice.

At g = 43, the weights are a = 31/2069 and b = 32/2069. Check: 43·31 + 23·32 = 1333 + 736 = 2069, so the weights sum to 1. The balanced load is 32·31/2069 = 992/2069.

The selector cannot do better. Every assignment m in [1312, 1376] forces some color to exceed 992/2069. Other (p, q) pairs, such as (33,31) or (33,30), give strictly smaller loads. Configurations with three or more weight groups are capped by Cauchy–Schwarz at 95/198 ≈ 0.4798, and integrality keeps the true optimum at 992/2069 ≈ 0.4796, just below that bound.

Debater A's 31/66 ≈ 0.4697 is below the value this construction already guarantees. The adversary can force 992/2069, so 31/66 cannot be the smallest constant C.
